summary: This informational document lists requirements for a service that lets applications subscribe to updates of a YANG datastore. Once a subscription is negotiated, changes are pushed to the chosen recipients instead of the application polling over and over. It points out that existing YANG transports such as NETCONF and RESTCONF lack this publish and subscribe capability.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking your friend every five minutes whether they have news, you ask them to text you when something changes. This lists what a text-me-when-it-changes service for network device settings must be able to do.

subtitle: What a push-based subscription service for YANG datastores must do, so applications stop polling network devices.

tldr.problem: Applications that need a continuous view of network device data, such as service assurance and security tools, have had to poll YANG datastores. Polling loads networks and devices and is brittle when cycles are missed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements for a subscription service: a subscriber negotiates what data it wants, how often or on what change, with which filters and quality of service, and the publisher then pushes updates to a receiver.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a protocol. It fills a gap in NETCONF and RESTCONF, which lack publish and subscribe, and sets terms for whatever solution follows.

today: RFC 7923 is an Informational requirements document and no obsoleting or updating RFC is listed for it. It states requirements rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Why Polling Is Not Enough
sections.content:
Some applications need more than the traditional client-server style of configuring network elements. Service-assurance applications must keep a continuous view of operational data and state, and security applications must keep tracking changes made to network elements to check compliance with policy.

The RFC says periodic fetching is not adequate for frequent or prompt updates. It loads networks, devices and applications, is brittle when communication glitches happen, and makes it hard to synchronize and calibrate retrieval intervals across a network. The proposed remedy is a generic subscription mechanism inside network elements, applied to data in YANG datastores.

The business drivers section adds that push mechanisms will supplement existing protocols rather than replace them. SNMP and MIBs will remain widely deployed for many monitoring solutions, but SNMP's reliance on polling is its biggest shortcoming for these applications.
sections.eli5: Checking again and again wastes effort and can miss things. It is better if the device tells you when something changes.

sections.title: Where Pub/Sub Already Appears
sections.content:
The document points to the Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) as a driver, citing requirements in RFC 7921 and in an I2RS use-case draft for things like near real-time notification of route installation and removal, and subscriptions to BGP, IGP and LDP events. RFC 7922 adds a requirement to publish I2RS trace logs to a feed.

It also says the work is meant to reach beyond I2RS, and notes past and present forms of subscription in multicast setup, SACM, MPLS VPNs (RFC 6513) and OSPF (RFC 2328). Because the underlying transports vary, a generalized mechanism should support alternative transports. NETCONF should be the initial transport because I2RS needs connection-oriented, unicast communication, with multicast and broadcast distribution needed eventually.

TIBCO, RSS and CORBA are called precursors that do not serve the new needs. XMPP and DDS come close and serve as proof-points that a scalable distributed implementation connecting millions of edge devices is possible.
sections.eli5: Many network tools already do a bit of sign-up-and-be-told. The RFC wants one general way to do it for device data.

sections.title: The Cast: Subscriber, Publisher and Receiver
sections.content:
A Subscriber asks for sets of YANG object data. A Publisher, generally the owner of the datastore, distributes that data under the terms of the subscription. A Receiver is the target that updates are pushed to; usually it is the same entity as the Subscriber. The Subscription Service provides subscriptions and works with the Publisher.

A subscription is a contract between the service and the Subscriber about what data is pushed and on what terms. An Update carries object changes in subscribed subtrees and may bundle ordered changes made since the last update. A Filter is either a subtree filter or a filter on object elements and attributes.

The RFC uses RFC 2119 words (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) even though it is not a protocol specification, to give clear instructions to people designing solutions.
sections.eli5: One side signs up, one side holds the news, and a third spot (often the same as the first) gets the delivery.

sections.title: Core Service Requirements
sections.content:
The service MUST be able to create, renew, time out and terminate subscriptions, track several subscriptions from one Subscriber independently, and support subscriptions on operational datastores, configuration datastores, or both. It MUST support periodic updates with a configurable period, and SHOULD support on-change updates. On-change updates MUST support a dampening period, SHOULD have it configurable, and MUST only send deltas, marking each object as removed, added or changed.

Negotiable terms MUST include the policy (on-change or periodic), the interval, the dampening period and any filters. If a request cannot be met, the service SHOULD hint at acceptable criteria, such as a longer interval. The service MAY revoke or suspend a subscription (for example for resource limits or credential expiry) but MUST then notify the Subscriber.

Other points: multiple objects SHOULD be bundled into one Update; an Update MUST NOT be sent before the dampening period ends, nor delayed beyond it or the Push Latency; a replay capability is optional. After a suspension, the first on-change update SHOULD include changes made during it, and the service MUST clearly say when that is not supported. Subscribers SHOULD avoid duplicate subscriptions to the same subtrees, MUST be able to tell when the service is no longer active, and MUST be able to lease and extend the lease of a subscription.
sections.eli5: You can ask for a report on a timer or only when something changes, and you can say how often at most. If it breaks, you must be told.

sections.title: Transport, QoS and Filtering
sections.content:
Updates may travel over NETCONF, RESTCONF, HTTP and emerging protocols, so the service SHOULD support different transports and payload encodings, and receivers MUST be able to tie an update to a subscription. With connection-oriented transport, a dropped connection SHOULD end the subscription, and the Subscriber must ask again.

For quality of service, the service SHOULD negotiate dampening, reliability, deadline and bundling. Updates for a subscription MUST arrive in sequential order, an administrator MUST be able to determine push latency, and subscriptions SHOULD support relative priority for when bandwidth is short.

Filtering MUST allow subtree and attribute filters. Mandatory types: for strings, equal, not equal or contains; for numbers, =, !=, <, <=, > or >=. Filters SHOULD be able to combine several properties and query other objects (for example, push A if A changed and B=1). Finally, it MUST be possible to fetch the state of one subscription, of all of a Subscriber's subscriptions, and a history of requests, with failure reasons such as bad credentials, a missing node or no resources.
sections.eli5: You can pick how the news arrives, how fast, and which pieces you care about, like only numbers bigger than a limit.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC puts its security rules in the requirements and says the formal Security Considerations section adds nothing beyond them. For privacy-sensitive deployments subscription information MUST be bound within secure, encrypted transport; with NETCONF, RFC 7589 is an option. Mutual authentication between Subscriber and service MUST be used, and subscribers MUST NOT be able to pose as the service.

Pushed data MUST be authorized the same way as on-demand retrieval, so unauthorized objects are filtered out. Changes in a subscribed subtree MUST be validated against authorization before being pushed, and requests to create, terminate, suspend or resume MUST be authorized. When Subscriber and Receiver differ, the Receiver MUST be able to end a unicast subscription to it. The service SHOULD decline a request that would likely exhaust its resources, preferably at the start.
sections.eli5: The service must check who you are, send you only what you are allowed to see, and not let anyone pretend to be it.
